name: Rosemary oil
lead: Rosemary oil is the essential oil steam-distilled from the leaves of the rosemary plant (Salvia rosmarinus, formerly Rosmarinus officinalis), long used in traditional medicine, perfumery and cooking.[1][15] In appearance communities it is applied to the scalp, and sometimes to eyebrows and lashes, with the aim of thicker-looking hair, and it is frequently described as a natural alternative or add-on to minoxidil.[2][3]

People use it by diluting a few drops in a carrier oil or adding it to shampoos, scalp masks or sprays, often with scalp massage, and many report using it for months before judging results.[17][18][19] Hair that looks fuller, a calmer scalp and a lower-risk routine than prescription treatments are the effects users typically describe.[13][18]

The main clinical evidence is a 2015 randomised trial of 100 people with androgenetic alopecia comparing rosemary oil with 2% minoxidil for six months; hair counts rose significantly in both groups from baseline with no significant difference between them.[4] Reviews generally count rosemary oil among natural products that may be considered, while describing the small number and limited quality of studies.[5][6][7] A 2025 Canadian consensus statement of eleven physicians listed rosemary oil among interventions it did not recommend for androgenetic alopecia.[8] The oil has also spread widely through TikTok and other social media, where #hairtok videos are reported to have drawn over a billion views.[18][19]
infobox: Camphor (roughly 10 to 20 percent), alpha-pinene, 1,8-cineole, rosmarinic and carnosic acid in extracts[15]
Hair growth and thickness (androgenetic alopecia); brows and lashes
2015 randomised trial vs 2% minoxidil, n=100, six months[4]
Cosmetic / aromatherapy product; not an approved hair-loss drug

paras: Rosemary was regarded as sacred by the ancient Egyptians, Greeks and Romans, was described by Pliny the Elder and Dioscorides, and appears in Shakespeare as a symbol of remembrance; Hungary water, a 14th-century alcohol-based perfume, was made primarily from it.[15] Wikipedia's essential oil article reports about 150 phytochemicals in the oil, including camphor at roughly 10 to 20 percent, rosmarinic acid, carnosic acid, carnosol and alpha-pinene, and the oil appears in perfumes, shampoos, cleaning products and aromatherapy.[15]

Its modern use as a hair product is tied to the 2015 SkinMed trial. Dermatologist Shilpi Khetarpal of Cleveland Clinic said, as quoted by WebMD, that the study prompted people to look at rosemary oil, and that it has since become much more common in over-the-counter products.[19] Earlier laboratory work on a rosemary leaf extract in a hair-growth model, by Murata and colleagues in 2013, is the usual source for the claim that rosemary blocks 5-alpha-reductase, the enzyme that makes DHT; one commentator notes that this work used an ethanol extract rather than essential oil.[17]

Rosemary oil is used on the scalp for hair thinning and, by some forum users, mixed with castor oil on eyebrows and lashes.[9] Reviews of natural alternatives for androgenetic alopecia highlight it as having gained popularity as a possible alternative to minoxidil and finasteride.[2][5]

Three explanations circulate. The first is that rosemary compounds inhibit 5-alpha-reductase, as finasteride does; this traces to the extract work noted above, and the blogger who reviewed it found the concentrations required high relative to finasteride and the active compound likely absent from the essential oil.[17] The second is improved scalp microcirculation: dermatologist Ryan Turner told PureWow that terpenes may relax blood vessels and increase scalp blood flow, similar to minoxidil, though not specific to rosemary, and that massage can also improve circulation.[18] The third is antioxidant and antimicrobial activity, which Turner suggested might help dandruff linked to Malassezia yeast, though he said he would more often recommend other products.[18] Doctors interviewed in coverage say the mechanism is not established.[17][18]

The 2015 randomised comparative trial assigned 50 participants to rosemary oil and 50 to 2% minoxidil. No significant change in hair count was observed at three months in either group; at six months both groups showed significant increases over baseline and over the three-month point, with no significant difference between them.[4] Grokipedia adds that the rosemary group was reported to have less scalp itching, and describes a 2025 Indian trial of rosemary blends with coconut oil as placebo; it notes that this used multi-ingredient blends with a small sample and short follow-up.[1]

A systematic review of natural products for male androgenetic alopecia found eleven clinical studies and concluded that rosemary oil, among others, might be considered in treatment.[5] A review of complementary supplements said rosemary oil was effective compared with baseline or minoxidil but called for more research.[7] A review of topical hair-growth actives noted that such agents have mostly been studied in combination formulations with small samples, lack of comparison with standard therapy and conflicts of interest.[3] The Canadian consensus, using a Delphi process, did not recommend rosemary oil.[8]

Reviewers outside the journal literature have raised design questions about the 2015 trial. Writing on a skincare-science site, Michelle Wong noted the comparator was 2% rather than the standard 5% minoxidil, that six months is early, that there was no placebo group, that average gains were small (about 6 hairs for rosemary and 2 for minoxidil), and that baseline and month-3 counts were identical.[17] PureWow quotes Dr. Ryan Turner saying the small hair-count gains make real effectiveness difficult to interpret.[18] Supporters note that the rosemary group reported less scalp itching than the minoxidil group.[4][19]

The principal hair study is the 2015 randomised trial against minoxidil 2% (n=100, six months).[4] Other registered or published human trials of rosemary oil concern unrelated uses, such as inhalation for shift-working nurses' alertness, topical use in Raynaud's phenomenon in systemic sclerosis, and a topical phytoterpene mixture for plantar fasciitis.[10][11][12] The trial randomised 100 men with androgenetic alopecia to rosemary oil or 2% minoxidil; both groups gained hair count by six months, with no significant difference, and the rosemary group reported less scalp itching.[4][19] A 2025 trial using rosemary blends with coconut oil as placebo is described by Grokipedia, with multi-ingredient blends, a small sample and short follow-up.[1]

Essential oils can contain irritants and allergens; camphor, carnosol and cineole have been named as possible triggers for some people, and in the 2015 trial scalp itching and dandruff were reported in the rosemary group.[17] Experts quoted by PureWow advise against applying undiluted oil, mention contact dermatitis, and say people with epilepsy, high blood pressure or pregnancy should avoid it; they suggest seeing a dermatologist first for hair loss and using rosemary oil as a supplement to prescribed treatment.[18] Khetarpal's routine as quoted by WebMD is massage into the scalp, leaving it on and washing out two or three times a week, with results taking around six months.[19] Rosemary oil is sold as a cosmetic or aromatherapy product, not an approved hair-loss drug.[1]

Rosemary oil is one of the most visible natural hair products on social media. PureWow reports 1.3 billion views on TikTok's #Hairtok for rosemary oil, with users crediting it for hair after chemotherapy, baldness and texture, and WebMD reports that #rosemaryoil videos have drawn over two billion views.[18][19] Dermatologists quoted in this coverage generally describe minoxidil as the better-supported option and rosemary oil as a possible adjunct.[18][19][17]

On looksmax.org, the minoxidil comparison abstract has been reposted, with one reply saying nobody would read it.[13] Another thread discusses rosemary oil's effect on gene expression with a hypothesis of histone deacetylase inhibition, and a reply says rosemary eaten in food was reported to block testosterone; a respondent asked whether washing the face with it would differ.[14] In a thread on castor and rosemary oil for brows and lashes, a reply says there is no strong evidence it works, that applying it does no harm, and that it acts somewhat like mascara, while another recommends oral minoxidil instead.[9]

In castor-oil threads on looksmax.org, users also ask whether castor and rosemary oil differ and how to mix them for eyebrows.[20][21] A further looksmax.org thread asks whether rosemary oil has worked for anyone, a recurring request for first-hand reports.[22]

lore.intro: Rosemary oil is discussed in hair-loss and grooming forums as a natural, low-risk minoxidil alternative.[9][13]

claims.claim: Rosemary oil works about as well as minoxidil
claims.believers: Forum users repost the 2015 trial abstract showing similar hair-count gains in both groups.[13]
claims.experts: The trial found no significant difference between groups at six months, but reviews describe the evidence base as small, and a Canadian consensus did not recommend rosemary oil.[4][3][8]

claims.claim: Rosemary oil regulates hundreds of genes, possibly acting as an HDAC inhibitor
claims.believers: A looksmax.org poster argued that rosemary oil is likely a broad histone deacetylase inhibitor with wide effects on gene expression.[14]
claims.experts: The reviewed sources contain no human study testing this mechanism for hair growth.

claims.claim: Castor oil plus rosemary oil thickens eyebrows and lashes
claims.believers: Some users say the combination works, others that it mainly coats the hairs like mascara.[9]
claims.experts: No published trial of this combination for brows or lashes appears in the reviewed literature.

claims.believers: One forum user said they learned that rosemary blocks testosterone.[14]
claims.experts: The reviewed sources do not include human data on this claim.

claims.claim: Rosemary oil blocks DHT like finasteride
claims.believers: Social media posts and some clinicians cite laboratory work on rosemary extract as evidence of 5-alpha-reductase inhibition.[17]
claims.experts: The cited work used an ethanol leaf extract in lab and animal models, and one reviewer argues the active compound is unlikely to be present in the essential oil.[17]

claims.claim: It improves scalp circulation, which grows hair
claims.believers: Users and some dermatologists describe a blood-flow effect similar to minoxidil, and scalp massage during application is part of the routine.[18]
claims.experts: Dermatologist Ryan Turner says terpenes may increase scalp blood flow but that this is not specific to rosemary oil; no trial has isolated the effect.[18]

claims.claim: Rosemary oil is gentler than minoxidil
claims.believers: The 2015 trial reported less scalp itching with rosemary oil, which supporters cite.[4][19]
claims.experts: Reviews describe a minimal side-effect profile, while experts warn that undiluted oil can irritate and cause contact dermatitis.[2][18]

card.summary: The natural minoxidil alternative: one small 2015 trial matched 2% minoxidil, but reviews call the evidence thin and a Canadian consensus did not recommend it.
card.note: Essential oil; evidence rests largely on one 100-person trial.

quick.overview:
Rosemary oil is a plant essential oil applied to the scalp (and sometimes brows) as a natural hair-growth aid. It is popular as a minoxidil alternative.
A 2015 trial of 100 people found similar hair-count gains to 2% minoxidil after six months. Reviews describe the evidence as limited, and a 2025 Canadian consensus did not recommend it.
quick.mechanism: Proposed explanations include improved microcirculation, and some forum users suggest effects on gene expression; neither is established for hair growth.
quick.risks: Reviews describe a minimal side-effect profile; the 2015 trial reported scalp itching less often than with minoxidil per Grokipedia. It is sold as a cosmetic or aromatherapy product rather than an approved hair-loss drug.
